citations.review_text: The airboat section makes me very angry please do not do this again thank you

Yeah, I'm one of the 5 people in the world who didn't like HL2. I liked Half-Life 1 because of the environmental storytelling, feeling of discovery, and the game letting you play at your own tempo. I actually liked the City 17 intro — poking through people's apartments, talking to NPCs, interacting with items. But I dropped HL2 because the canals section was just very boring for me. Go forward, shoot, puzzle, repeat. No room to explore and find something interesting. I watched the full playthrough of the game a couple years ago and the feelings were the same even later into the game, so I stopped playing early. Technically it's great, just not for me.

Over 20 years later, and this game holds up remarkably well. I made an initial playthrough a couple years ago, but I stopped at Anticitizen One because I am on Linux and the game kept crashing at this section, so I couldn't go any further. Fortunately, I was able to complete the game this time and its two subsequent episodes.

The totalitarian dystopia has its clear inspirations from sci-fi novels and movies, especially if we were to look at earlier phases of the game's development. At the same time, Valve has taken plenty of changes to transform it from a mere adaptation to something with its own, unique identity. It carefully transitions its prior lore and gameplay into something that makes it a perfect sequel for both returning players and those who have never played the first game, something that is extremely difficult to pull off. Not just through its plot, but also through its world building and innovation of mechanics that at the time, were groundbreaking.

The game is a masterpiece, but it isn't without its flaws. There were certain points in the game where I did struggle a little bit with navigation, and not to mention that the "Anticitizen One" and "Follow Freeman!" chapters were a bit of a struggle with overall progression, as I did start utilizing save states because I just kept making mistakes and some of the puzzles and combat were quite tough. The squad AI does its best for its time, but there have been points where the bodyblocking becomes an inconvenience and my squad mates will sometimes just return to me even though I told them to go someplace (and they end up dying as a result).

On top of that, the physics engine is a remarkable feat, but over 20 years later, it does have its moments where it shows its age (especially with the initial antlion section where I kept having to fidget with the gravity gun to get props in the place I want them to). I would call this the best Singleplayer game of all time (imo). This game is a classic. Everything feels perfect, and the revolutionary physics are pretty fun to mess around with the gravity gun. When it goes stale, just visit the workshop and the experience becomes refreshing again. Also has a supportive modding community (thankyou!) that has kept the game relevant for ~20 years. 20/10 must play

Still one of the best games of all time. The use of physics in solving problems and using the environment to maximum effect is amazing. Super fun. Launch a gnome into space.

The flow from level to level remains fantastic to this day. It's a game that feels like one continuous journey, through naturalistic levels that immerse you yet give you epic challenges to overcome. The systemic nature of the game, blending physics with gunplay, enhances the combat even when you aren't deliberately limiting yourself to the gravity gun. It feels like a game that wants you to play around with it, screw around with how objects can fly around when propelled, yet blends that into the ways you engage with combat rather than leaving it all as optional or superfluous sandbox mechanics.
